column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 14: The sanctity of a Muslim's blood

column2: ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “The blood of a Muslim is not lawful except in one of three cases: the married adulterer, a life for a life, and the one who abandons his religion and separates from the community.”
Al-Bukhārī and Muslim reported it.

This hadith is recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs by way of al-Aʿmash, from ʿAbdullāh ibn Murrah, from Masrūq, from Ibn Masʿūd. One narration of Muslim's has “the one who abandons Islam” in place of “his religion”.
There are a number of hadiths with this meaning. Muslim recorded, from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah, from the Prophet ﷺ, the like of Ibn Masʿūd's hadith.

Al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah recorded, from the hadith of ʿUthmān, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The blood of a Muslim is not lawful except in one of three cases: a man who disbelieves after accepting Islam, or commits adultery after marriage, or kills a soul other than in return for a soul.”

In one narration of al-Nasāʾī's: “A man who commits adultery after marriage is to be stoned; one who kills deliberately is liable to retaliation; and one who apostatises after accepting Islam is to be put to death.”
This meaning has also been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ in the narrations of Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Hurayrah, Anas and others. We have already cited the hadith of Anas,

which explains that these three traits are the right of Islam by which the blood of one who testifies that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah becomes lawful. Killing for each one of these three traits is agreed upon among the Muslims.

As for adultery by a married person, the Muslims are unanimous that its prescribed punishment (ḥadd) is stoning until death. The Prophet ﷺ stoned Māʿiz and the Ghāmidī woman. Among the verses of the Qurʾān whose wording was abrogated was: “The old man and the old woman, if they commit adultery, stone them both outright, as an exemplary punishment from Allah; and Allah is Mighty, Wise.”

Ibn ʿAbbās derived stoning from the Qurʾān, from the words of the Exalted: “O People of the Book, Our Messenger has come to you, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Book, and passing over much” [al-Māʾidah 5:15].
He said: Whoever disbelieves in stoning has disbelieved in the Qurʾān without realising it. Then he recited this verse and said: Stoning was among what they concealed.
Al-Nasāʾī recorded it, as did al-Ḥākim, who said: Its chain is authentic.

It is also derived from the words of the Exalted: “We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light; by it the prophets who submitted [to Allah] judged for those who were Jews…” up to His words: “and that you should judge between them by what Allah has sent down” [al-Māʾidah 5:44–49].
Al-Zuhrī said: We have been told that it was revealed about the two Jews whom the Prophet ﷺ stoned. He said, “I judge by what is in the Torah,” and gave orders concerning them, and they were stoned.
Muslim recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ, from the hadith of al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib, the story of the stoning of the two Jews, and in his hadith he said: Then Allah revealed:

“O Messenger, do not let those who hasten into disbelief grieve you” [al-Māʾidah 5:41], and He revealed: “Whoever does not judge by what Allah has sent down — it is they who are the disbelievers” [al-Māʾidah 5:44] — all of these verses concern the disbelievers.

Imam Aḥmad recorded it, and his version has: Then Allah revealed: “Do not let those who hasten into disbelief grieve you…” up to His words: “If you are given this, take it” [al-Māʾidah 5:41]. They were saying: Go to Muḥammad;

if he gives you a ruling of blackening the face and flogging, take it, and if he gives you a ruling of stoning, beware — up to His words: “Whoever does not judge by what Allah has sent down — it is they who are the disbelievers” [al-Māʾidah 5:44]. He said: This is about the Jews.
The story of the stoning of the two Jews has also been narrated from the hadith of Jābir, and in his hadith he said: Then Allah revealed:
“If they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them…” up to His words: “and if you judge, judge between them with justice” [al-Māʾidah 5:42].

At first Allah the Exalted had commanded that women who commit fornication be confined until death takes them or Allah ordains a way for them; then Allah ordained a way for them. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, ʿUbādah narrated

that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Take it from me, take it from me: Allah has ordained a way for them. For the unmarried with the unmarried, a hundred lashes and a year's banishment; for the married with the married, a hundred lashes and stoning.”

A group of scholars took this hadith at face value and required that the married offender be given a hundred lashes and then stoned, as ʿAlī did with Shurāḥah al-Hamdāniyyah. He said: I flogged her by the Book of Allah and stoned her by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

He meant that the Book of Allah contains the flogging of the man and woman who commit fornication, without distinguishing married from unmarried, and that the Sunnah came with stoning for the married in particular — though stoning is also derived from the Qurʾān.
This is the well-known view of Imam Aḥmad (may Allah have mercy on him) and of Isḥāq, and it is the view of al-Ḥasan and a group of the Salaf.
Another group of them said: If the two married offenders are old, they are stoned and flogged; if they are young, they are stoned without flogging,

because an old man's sin is the more hideous, especially in fornication. This is the view of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb. It has also been narrated from him as marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ), but it is not authentic as marfūʿ. It is also a reported position of Aḥmad, and of Isḥāq.
As for “a life for a life”, it means that when a legally responsible person kills someone deliberately and without right, he is killed for it. The Qurʾān indicates this in the words of the Exalted:

“We prescribed for them therein: a life for a life” [al-Māʾidah 5:45]. The Exalted also said: “O you who believe, retaliation is prescribed for you in cases of killing: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female” [al-Baqarah 2:178].
Certain cases are excepted from the general sense of His words, “a life for a life”.
One of them is a father killing his child. The majority hold that he is not killed for him, and this is authentically reported from ʿUmar.

It has also been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ through numerous routes, though their chains have been criticised. Mālik said: If he meant to kill him with an intent about which there is no doubt, such as by slaughtering him, he is killed for him; but if he struck him by throwing a sword or a stick at him, he is not killed.
Al-Battī said: He is killed for killing him in every form of deliberate killing, because of the general texts.
Another is a free man killing a slave. Most hold that he is not killed for him, and there are hadiths on this whose chains have been criticised.

It has been said that he is killed for someone else's slave but not for his own; this is the view of Abū Ḥanīfah and his companions. It has also been said that he is killed for his own slave and for someone else's alike; this is one reported view of al-Thawrī and the view of a group of the hadith scholars,
because of the hadith of Samurah, from the Prophet ﷺ: “Whoever kills his slave, we will kill him; and whoever mutilates him, we will mutilate him.” Imam Aḥmad and others have impugned it.

They are unanimous that there is no retaliation between slaves and free men for injuries to the limbs, and this shows that this hadith has been set aside and is not acted upon. This is also used as evidence that what is meant by His words “a life for a life” is free persons,
because after it He mentions retaliation for the limbs, which applies only to free persons.
Another is a Muslim killing a disbeliever. If the disbeliever is a combatant (ḥarbī), the Muslim is not killed for him — on this there is no disagreement —

because killing a combatant is undoubtedly permissible. If he is a dhimmī or under a covenant (muʿāhad), the majority hold that he is not killed for him either. In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, ʿAlī narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “A Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever.”

Abū Ḥanīfah and a group of the jurists of al-Kūfah said that he is killed for him. Rabīʿah narrated, from Ibn al-Baylamānī, that the Prophet ﷺ had a man of the people of the qiblah killed for a man of the protected people (ahl al-dhimmah), and said:

“I am the most entitled to fulfil his pledge of protection.” This is a weak mursal hadith. Imam Aḥmad, Abū ʿUbayd, Ibrāhīm al-Ḥarbī, al-Jūzajānī, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Dāraquṭnī declared it weak, and al-Dāraquṭnī said: Ibn al-Baylamānī is weak and no proof can be established by him even when he gives a hadith with a connected chain, so what of one he narrates mursal?
Al-Jūzajānī said: Rabīʿah took it only from Ibrāhīm ibn Abī Yaḥyā, from Ibn al-Munkadir, from Ibn al-Baylamānī; and Ibn Abī Yaḥyā is abandoned as a narrator (matrūk al-ḥadīth).

In the Marāsīl of Abū Dāwūd there is another mursal hadith: that on the day of Khaybar the Prophet ﷺ had a Muslim killed for a disbeliever whom he had killed treacherously (ghīlah), and said: “I am the most worthy and the most entitled to fulfil his pledge of protection.”

This is the school of Mālik and the people of Madīnah: treacherous killing does not require equivalence [between killer and victim], so in such a case a Muslim is killed for a disbeliever. On this basis they also interpreted the hadith of Ibn al-Baylamānī, supposing it to be authentic.
Another is a man killing a woman. He is killed for her, without disagreement. In the letter of ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm, from the Prophet ﷺ: a man is killed for a woman.
It is authentically reported that he ﷺ had a Jew killed who had killed a girl. Most scholars hold that when a man is killed for a woman, nothing is paid to his next of kin.
It has been narrated from ʿAlī that half the blood money is paid to them,
because a woman's blood money is half a man's. This is the view of a group of the Salaf, and of Aḥmad in one reported position.

As for “the one who abandons his religion and separates from the community”, what is meant is whoever abandons Islam, apostatises from it and separates from the community of the Muslims, as is stated explicitly in the hadith of ʿUthmān.
He is counted among the people of the two testimonies whose blood becomes lawful only in view of what he was before his apostasy, since the ruling of Islam still binds him afterwards.

That is why he is called on to repent and asked to return to Islam. Whether he is obliged to make up the acts of worship he missed during his apostasy is a well-known point of disagreement among scholars.

Moreover, someone may abandon his religion and separate from the community while still affirming the two testimonies and claiming Islam: for example, if he denies one of the pillars of Islam, or reviles Allah and His Messenger,

or disbelieves in some of the angels, prophets or scriptures mentioned in the Qurʾān while knowing of them. In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Ibn ʿAbbās narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.”

Most scholars make no distinction in this between man and woman. Some, however, said: A woman is not killed if she apostatises, just as the women of the enemy's land (dār al-ḥarb) are not killed in war, only their men. This is the view of Abū Ḥanīfah and his companions,

who treated disbelief that arises later like original disbelief. The majority distinguished between them and held later disbelief to be graver than original disbelief, because of the Islam that preceded it. That is why apostasy from Islam is punished by death even in those who would not be killed if they were among the enemy, such as the decrepit old man, the chronically disabled and the blind, who are not killed in war.
His words ﷺ, “the one who abandons his religion and separates from the community”, show that if he repented and returned to Islam he would not be killed,
since after his return he is neither abandoning his religion nor separating from the community.

If it is said: On the contrary, his being excepted from the people of the two testimonies whose blood is protected shows that he is killed even if he affirms the two testimonies, just as the married adulterer and the killer are; and this shows that the apostate's repentance is not accepted, as is reported from al-Ḥasan;
or else it is to be taken as referring to someone born a Muslim who apostatises, whose repentance is not accepted — repentance being accepted only from one who was a disbeliever,
then accepted Islam, then apostatised, according to the view of a group of scholars, among them al-Layth ibn Saʿd, Aḥmad in one reported position, and Isḥāq —
the reply is: he excepted him from the Muslims only in view of what he was before leaving his religion, as was established above. He is not like the married adulterer and the killer,
because killing those two became due as a punishment for a crime already committed, and there is no way of undoing that.

The apostate, by contrast, is killed only because of a quality present in him at the time: abandoning his religion and separating from the community. If he returns to his religion and to agreement with the community, the quality for which his blood was made lawful is gone, and so the lawfulness of his blood ceases. And Allah knows best.
If it is said: Al-Nasāʾī recorded, from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The blood of a Muslim is not lawful except for one of three traits:

a married adulterer, who is stoned; a man who kills deliberately, who is killed; and a man who leaves Islam and wages war against Allah and His Messenger, who is killed, crucified or banished from the land.”
This shows that what is meant is someone who combines apostasy with waging war.

The reply is: Abū Dāwūd recorded the hadith of ʿĀʾishah in other words, namely that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “The blood of a Muslim who testifies that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah is not lawful except in one of three cases:

a man who commits adultery after marriage, who is stoned; a man who goes out waging war against Allah and His Messenger, who is killed, crucified or banished from the land; or one who kills a soul and is killed for it.”
This shows that when a Muslim is found to have waged war, the ruler may choose freely among the penalties for him, as the scholars of Madīnah, Mālik and others, hold.

The first narration may be taken to mean that “leaving Islam” is leaving the rulings of Islam; or it may be taken at face value. Those who say that the verse on waging war applies specifically to apostates cite it as evidence:
whoever apostatises and wages war is dealt with as the verse prescribes, while whoever wages war without apostasy is subject to the rulings for Muslims, such as retaliation and amputation for theft.

This is a reported position of Aḥmad, though not the well-known one. A group of the Salaf likewise said that the verse on waging war applies specifically to apostates, among them Abū Qilābah and others.

In any case, the wording of ʿĀʾishah's hadith varies, and it has been narrated from her both as marfūʿ and as mawqūf (as the Prophet's words and as her own), whereas there is no variation in the wording of Ibn Masʿūd's hadith,
which is firmly established and agreed to be authentic. Even so, it may be objected that the killing of a Muslim has been reported for things other than these three traits.
Among them is sodomy. From the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Kill the one who does it and the one to whom it is done.” Many scholars, such as Mālik and Aḥmad, adopted this and said

that it requires death in every case, whether the offender is married or not. It has been narrated that ʿUthmān said: The blood of a Muslim is not lawful except for one of four — and he mentioned the three above and added: and a man who does the deed of the people of Lūṭ.

Among them is one who has intercourse with a woman within the prohibited degrees. An order to kill him has been narrated, and it has been narrated that the Prophet ﷺ had a man killed who had married his father's wife. A group of scholars adopted this and required that he be killed in every case, whether married or not.

Among them is the sorcerer. In al-Tirmidhī, from the hadith of Jundub, as marfūʿ: “The prescribed punishment for the sorcerer is a stroke of the sword”; and al-Tirmidhī stated that it is correctly mawqūf on Jundub.

This is the school of a group of scholars, among them ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, Mālik, Aḥmad and Isḥāq; but they hold that he becomes a disbeliever by his sorcery, so that his ruling is that of apostates.
Among them is killing one who has intercourse with an animal. A marfūʿ hadith has come about it, and a group of scholars held this view.
Among them is one who abandons the prayer. Many scholars hold that he is killed, even though they say he is not a disbeliever. This has already been discussed in full.
Among them is killing the wine-drinker on the fourth occasion. The command to do so has come from the Prophet ﷺ through numerous routes,

and ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ and others adopted it, but most scholars hold that the killing has been abrogated. It has been narrated that the Prophet ﷺ was brought the drinker on the fourth occasion and did not kill him.
In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī: a man used to be brought to the Prophet ﷺ for drinking wine, and another man cursed him and said: How often he is brought! The Prophet ﷺ said: “Do not curse him,
for he loves Allah and His Messenger.” And he did not have him killed for it.
The killing of the thief on the fifth occasion has also been narrated, and it is said that some jurists held this view.

Among them is what has been narrated from him ﷺ, that he said: “If allegiance is pledged to two caliphs, kill the latter of them.” Muslim recorded it from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd. Al-ʿUqaylī declared weak all the hadiths on this subject.

Among them are his words ﷺ: “Whoever comes to you, when your affairs are united under one man, wanting to break your staff [of unity] or divide your community, kill him.” In one narration: “Strike his head with the sword, whoever he may be.”
Muslim recorded this too, from the narration of ʿArfajah.

Among them is one who draws a weapon. Al-Nasāʾī recorded, from the hadith of Ibn al-Zubayr, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever draws a weapon and then brings it down, his blood is forfeit.” It has been narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr both as marfūʿ and as mawqūf, and al-Bukhārī said: It is only mawqūf.
Aḥmad was asked about the meaning of this hadith, and he said: I do not know what this is.

Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh said: He means only someone who draws his weapon and then brings it down among the people, cutting them down indiscriminately; it has then become lawful to kill him. This is the way of the Ḥarūriyyah, who cut down men, women and children indiscriminately.

Something that goes against Isḥāq's explanation has been narrated from ʿĀʾishah. Al-Ḥākim recorded, from the narration of ʿAlqamah ibn Abī ʿAlqamah, from his mother, that a slave drew his sword on his master during the governorship of Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ and lunged at him with it, but the people held him back from him.

The master went in to see ʿĀʾishah, and she said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: “Whoever points an iron blade at any of the Muslims intending to kill him, his blood has become due.” So his master took him and killed him. Al-Ḥākim said: It is authentic according to the conditions of al-Bukhārī and Muslim.
It is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: “Whoever is killed defending his property is a martyr,” and in one narration: “Whoever is killed defending his life is a martyr.”
So when someone's property or life is targeted, he repels the attacker by the least severe means.
This is the school of al-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad. Must he intend that he does not want to kill him, or not?
There are two reported positions of Imam Aḥmad on this.

A group held that a man may kill outright, from the start, anyone who goes after his property or his life. A thief came in upon Ibn ʿUmar, and he rose against him with a drawn sword; had they not come between them, he would have killed him.

Al-Ḥasan was asked about a thief who entered a man's house carrying an iron blade, and he said: Kill him in whatever way you are able. These permitted killing him even if he turned and fled without having done any harm; among them was Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī.
Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The house is your sanctuary; whoever enters your sanctuary, kill him.” But there is weakness in its chain.

Among them is killing a Muslim spy who spies on the Muslims for the disbelievers. Aḥmad withheld judgement on it; a group of Mālik's followers permitted killing him, as did Ibn ʿAqīl among the scholars of our [Ḥanbalī] school. Some of the Mālikīs said: If he does it repeatedly,

killing him becomes permissible. Those who permit killing him cite the words of the Prophet ﷺ concerning Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Baltaʿah, when he wrote the letter to the people of Makkah informing them that the Prophet ﷺ was marching against them
and telling them to be on their guard. ʿUmar asked permission to kill him, and he said: “He was present at Badr.” He did not say that Ḥāṭib had done nothing to make his blood lawful;

rather, he gave as his reason the existence of something that prevented his being killed, namely his presence at Badr and Allah's forgiveness of the people of Badr — and this impediment does not exist for anyone after him.

Among them is what Abū Dāwūd recorded in al-Marāsīl from the narration of Ibn al-Musayyab: that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever strikes his father, kill him.” It has also been narrated with a connected chain by another route, which is not authentic.

Know that some of these hadiths we have mentioned are not authentic, and no scholar of standing is known to have held them, such as the hadith “Whoever strikes his father, kill him” and the hadith of killing the thief on the fifth occasion.
All the remaining texts can be traced back to Ibn Masʿūd's hadith. Ibn Masʿūd's hadith states that the blood of a Muslim is made lawful only by one of three traits:
either he abandons his religion and separates from the community of the Muslims, or he commits adultery while married, or he kills a soul without right.

From it one may infer that killing a Muslim is made lawful only by one of three kinds of act: abandoning the religion, shedding inviolable blood, and violating sexual sanctity. These three kinds, and nothing else, are what make a Muslim's blood lawful.

As for violating sexual sanctity, the hadith names it as fornication after marriage. This — and Allah knows best — is by way of example, for the married person has been granted in full the blessing of satisfying this desire through marriage; so if after that he satisfies it with someone forbidden to him,

his blood becomes lawful. The condition of marriage may be absent and be replaced by another condition: that the partner is one who can never be made lawful in any circumstances, either absolutely, as with sodomy, or for the one concerned, as with someone who has intercourse with a woman within the prohibited degrees, whether by a marriage contract or otherwise. Does this quality take the place of marriage and stand in for it?
This is the point of dispute among scholars, and the hadiths indicate that it does stand in for it and suffices to make the blood lawful.

As for shedding inviolable blood: does stirring up the strife that leads to bloodshed take its place — such as dividing the community of the Muslims, breaking its unity, pledging allegiance to a second ruler, or showing the disbelievers where the Muslims are vulnerable?
This is the point of dispute.
Something has been narrated from ʿUmar indicating that killing is permissible for things of this kind.
Likewise, does drawing a weapon with intent to kill take the place of killing in making blood lawful, or not?
Ibn al-Zubayr and ʿĀʾishah held that it takes the place of actual killing in this.
Likewise, does highway robbery in itself make killing permissible, or not,

given that it is a likely occasion for shedding inviolable blood? The words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, “Whoever kills a soul, other than for a soul or for corruption in the land, it is as though he had killed all mankind” [al-Māʾidah 5:32], show that taking a life is permissible only for one of two things:

one is in return for a life, and the other is for corruption in the land. Corruption in the land includes waging war, apostasy and fornication, for all of these are corruption in the land. Likewise, repeated wine-drinking and persisting in it is a likely occasion for shedding inviolable blood.

In the time of ʿUmar the Companions agreed on eighty lashes as its prescribed punishment, treating drunkenness as a likely occasion for slander and the false accusation of fornication (qadhf), which requires eighty lashes.

When the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays came to the Prophet ﷺ and he forbade them intoxicating drinks and steeping dates in [certain] vessels, he said: “One of you will get up and go to his cousin” — meaning,
when he has drunk — “and strike him with the sword.” Among them was a man who had received a wound in just that way,

and he used to hide it out of shyness before the Prophet ﷺ. All of this comes down to making blood lawful through killing, by treating the likely occasions of killing as if they were the thing itself. But has that been abrogated, or does its ruling still stand? This is the point of dispute.

As for abandoning the religion and separating from the community, it means apostasy from the religion of Islam, even if he still pronounces the two testimonies. If he reviled Allah and His Messenger ﷺ while affirming the two testimonies, his blood would become lawful,
because by doing so he has abandoned his religion.

The same applies if he treats the copy of the Qurʾān with contempt and throws it into filth, or denies something known by necessity to be part of the religion, such as the prayer, or anything else of that kind that takes one out of the religion.
Does abandoning one of the five pillars of Islam take its place?
This depends on whether doing so takes one out of the religion altogether or not.

Whoever regards it as leaving the religion treats it as equivalent to abandoning and denying the two testimonies. Those who do not regard it as leaving the religion differ over whether he is to be treated like one who abandons the religion as regards killing, because he has abandoned one of the foundations of Islam, or not,
because he has not left the religion.
Under the same heading comes what many scholars have said about killing those who call to innovations. They considered that this resembles leaving the religion

and is a means and path to it. If such a person keeps it hidden and does not call others to it, his ruling is that of the hypocrites when they keep themselves hidden; if he calls others to it, his crime becomes graver, because he is corrupting the religion of the community.
The command to fight and kill the Khawārij is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ.
Scholars have differed over their ruling.
Some said: They are disbelievers, so they are killed for their disbelief.

Some said: They are killed only for their corruption in the land, in shedding the blood of Muslims and declaring them disbelievers. This is the view of Mālik and a group of the scholars of our school, and they permitted initiating the fight against them and finishing off their wounded.

Some said: If they call others to what they hold, they are fought; if they display it but do not call to it, they are not fought. This is what Aḥmad and Isḥāq stated explicitly, and it comes back to fighting whoever calls to a grave innovation.

Some held that the fight should not be begun against them until they begin hostilities that make fighting them permissible, such as shedding blood and the like, as was narrated from ʿAlī. This is the view of al-Shāfiʿī and many of the scholars of our school.
It has been narrated through numerous routes that the Prophet ﷺ ordered a man who was praying to be killed, and said: “Had he been killed,

it would have been the first strife and the last.” In one narration: “Had he been killed, no two men of my community would have differed until the Dajjāl emerges.” Imam Aḥmad (may Allah have mercy on him) and others recorded it.
This is used as evidence for killing the innovator when killing him would keep his evil away from the Muslims and cut off the source of strife.
Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr and others reported that the school of Mālik permits killing one who calls to innovation.
So, understood in this way, all the texts about killing come back to what is in Ibn Masʿūd's hadith, and to Allah be the praise.
Many scholars say of many of the texts we have mentioned here that they were abrogated by Ibn Masʿūd's hadith. This is questionable in two respects.
First, it is not known that Ibn Masʿūd's hadith came later than all those texts, especially as Ibn Masʿūd was one of the earliest Emigrants,

while many of those texts are narrated by people who accepted Islam late, such as Abū Hurayrah, Jarīr ibn ʿAbdullāh and Muʿāwiyah; all of them narrated the hadith on killing the wine-drinker on the fourth occasion.
Second, the specific is not abrogated by the general, even if the general came after it, according to the correct view held by the majority of scholars,

because the specific indicates its meaning by explicit statement (naṣṣ), whereas the general indicates it only by apparent meaning (ẓāhir), according to most of them; and what is apparent does not cancel the ruling of what is explicit.
It has been narrated that the Prophet ﷺ ordered the killing of a man who lied about him during his lifetime. The man had said to a clan of the Arabs:
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ has sent me and commanded me to rule over your lives and property. This has been narrated through numerous routes, all of them weak.
Some of them state that this man had asked for the hand of one of their women in the Jāhiliyyah and they had refused to marry her to him; when he told them this, they believed him,
and he went and stayed with that woman. This man, then, had committed fornication and attributed its permissibility to the Prophet ﷺ, and that is disbelief and apostasy from the religion.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim:
the Prophet ﷺ ordered ʿAlī to kill the Copt who used to visit Māriyah, the mother of his child; people had been talking about it, but when ʿAlī found that he was a eunuch, he left him alone.

Some have explained it as meaning that the Copt had not yet accepted Islam, and that a person under covenant who does something that harms the Muslims breaks his covenant — so how much more so if he harms the Prophet ﷺ?
Others said: No, he was a Muslim, but he had been told to stop and did not, until people began to talk, because of him, about the Prophet's marital honour ﷺ;

and harming the Prophet ﷺ in his marital honour makes blood lawful. But when his innocence became plain for all to see, Māriyah's innocence became clear to the people, and the cause that made killing him lawful was removed.
It has been narrated from Imam Aḥmad that the Prophet ﷺ was entitled to kill for reasons other than the three in Ibn Masʿūd's hadith,
while no one else is. He seems to be indicating that he ﷺ was entitled to impose death as a discretionary punishment (taʿzīr) when he saw benefit in it,
because he ﷺ was protected from transgression and injustice, whereas no one else is entitled to do so,
since he cannot be trusted not to transgress out of his own desires.
Abū Dāwūd said: I heard Aḥmad being asked about the hadith of Abū Bakr, “That was not for anyone after the Prophet ﷺ.” He said: Abū Bakr was not entitled to kill a man except for one of three things,

whereas the Prophet ﷺ was entitled to kill. The hadith of Abū Bakr referred to is that a man spoke harshly to Abū Bakr, and Abū Barzah said to him: Shall I not kill him, O successor of the Messenger of Allah?
Abū Bakr said: That was not for anyone after the Prophet ﷺ.

This explains the hadith ordering the killing of the Copt, and it also explains the hadith ordering the killing of the thief, if that is authentic. That hadith says that the Prophet ﷺ ordered him killed the first time,

but they appealed to him about it, and he had his hand cut off instead. The same happened four times — he would order him killed, they would appeal to him, and a limb would be cut off — until all four of his limbs had been cut off; then he was killed on the fifth occasion. And Allah the Exalted knows best.
